title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Pet and house sitting
audience: Pet and house sitters who need a base day rate, a visit rate and a minimum charge before they quote.
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short jobs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on the work you offer, the local market and your experience. A sitter who offers visits, overnight stays and house sitting with a daily report can justify a higher rate, because the owner saves time. Vendor ranges show how wide the market is. Dogster lists at-home visits and walks at $25 to $45 per dog per day, and house sitting at $60 to $100 per day (vendor, 4 July 2026, updated 18 October 2026). A listing range shows what is offered; your costs set your floor. The same article gives dog sitting as around $80 to $150 a day, which conflicts with its own at-home row, so do not treat either range as settled.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Visits, overnight duties, travel between homes, admin, booking, marketing, training, vehicle upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid hours in a year, subtract the non-billable time, and you have billable hours. A Jobber guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours. That is a general range, not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it (Jobber Academy, 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, the vehicle, phone and booking fees, consumables, any registration fee and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (1 October 2026). Divide the total by billable hours. A pet-sitting association describes a method that sets a standard rate for each visit length of 30, 45 and 60 minutes (Pet Sitters International, July 2026). Its survey is not an Australian source, so use the method only. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation apply to you. Business Victoria recommends reviewing prices about every three months (no date shown on the page).

instruction.heading: Visit rates and day rates
instruction.body: Choose how you will charge: a standard rate for each visit length, a day rate for a set number of visits, or an overnight rate. Make the rule clear and write it down. A visit rate that assumes a 30-minute visit leaves out the drive. A Housecall Pro handyman guide, a vendor source, says drive time should be counted against the hourly rate (updated 21 October 2026). Count drive time in your figure, or add a travel charge that is stated in the price sheet.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: A short visit still pays for travel, set-up and admin. Set the minimum from the full cost of one visit, divided by one minus your target margin. A contractor pricing guide proposes this method and labels its own figures as illustrative (Contractor+, 23 September 2026). Tell the owner the minimum before the first booking. The same guide suggests one minimum for several small tasks in one visit, rather than a separate minimum for each task.

procedure: Estimate paid hours in a year, then subtract visit travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find billable hours.
List annual running costs, including insurance, vehicle, phone, booking fees, consumables and any registration fee.
Add the income you need, with on-costs and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate, then set visit-length rates and a day rate from it.
Set a minimum for one visit that covers travel and admin, and state it in writing.
Review the rates every quarter, and record each change and its reason.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only. A sitter can bill only 60 of every 100 paid hours. She prices a 30-minute visit as if all of her paid time were billable. The home is 20 minutes' drive away each way, so each visit uses about 70 minutes of her time, and she bills the 30 minutes on site.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect of pricing the visit from the 30 minutes on site, and how should the visit rate be built?
workedExamples.reasoning: Each visit uses 70 minutes of her time, but only 30 minutes are billed, so 40 minutes of each visit go unpaid. If the visit rate is set per billable hour without the drive, the rate is too low. She builds the rate from billable hours, counts the drive time (or adds a stated travel charge), and sets a minimum for a short visit that covers the trip. If her costs need a fixed amount per billable hour, every billable minute must carry the cost of about 70 minutes of her time, which is 70 divided by 30, or about 2.33 minutes of cost per minute billed.

equipmentAndPpe: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Log of paid, billable and travel time for one month
Price sheet with visit-length rates, a day rate, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting rates from a listing range or a competitor's price without checking your costs
commonErrors.prevention: Build the rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local listings.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time, including drive time, before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Charging one visit rate for a short visit and a long one, without covering travel
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum that covers travel and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited (15 July 2026). The sources read do not cover minimum or call-out charges or what counts as a fair term; check that before you publish a price sheet.
Tax treatment of leave, superannuation and self-employed income is UNCONFIRMED. Confirm it with a registered tax agent.
Victorian rules for in-home pet sitting are UNRESOLVED. Check a price sheet for a Victorian service with the council before you publish it.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, including drive time.
The base rate is built from costs and an income target, and compared with local listings.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions, including travel
Price sheet with visit rates, day rate, minimum charge and review date
summary: Price from billable hours, including drive time, not from paid hours.
Build the rates from costs and an income target, then check them against local listings.
Set and state a minimum for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A sitter can bill only some of her paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and the owner pays less
From billable hours, so costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average day rate on a platform and the nearest sitter's rate
From the rate the sitter would like the market to pay

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up or admin at all
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the length of the visit
Because owners expect every visit to cost the same, whatever its length
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every booking

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single vendor's average day rate from a website
Your own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate without checking costs or the local market
The price on the first page of a platform this week
